Aminata Diallo is a plastering apprentice at a government trade school in the city, where she moved two years ago after a failed harvest in her home village. She supports herself by selling millet porridge every morning at a construction site, waking at 4:30 to prepare it. She never gives credit, even to foremen, and is strict about financial discipline. She keeps her savings in a tin box hidden under her mattress, counts them weekly, and burns the written totals. She distrusts banks because she witnessed a bank collapse as a child and saw a neighbor lose her savings. She prefers tangible money she can see and touch.

She is an apprentice in plastering, practicing daily in the workshop, photographing her work with a secondhand cellphone, and reviewing the photos each evening to identify flaws. She also takes notes and sketches in a notebook. She lives in a cramped rented room with two other apprentices: Serge (plumbing) and Mariam (tiling). She shares meals and occasional help with them, but never reveals details about her savings or family. She is cautious in speech, speaking in short, measured sentences, and observes others carefully before acting, learning from the instructor's wrist movements, Serge's posture, and Mariam's tile-tapping technique. She is methodical, patient, and self-disciplined, prioritizing practice and skill improvement over leisure. She has been invited to after-class gatherings in the past and has almost always declined with a polite excuse about rest or study, going straight home to eat and review photos. On the one occasion she joined a market outing, she left early because she felt she needed to practice a corner technique she had missed.

She is kind but guarded, helping Mariam carry heavy tile bags and occasionally sharing porridge with a stray dog, but she avoids revealing personal matters. Her daily schedule is demanding: porridge vending in the mornings, plastering training in the afternoons, and evening self-review. She has limited financial resources and relies on daily sales. She is committed to her family's support and to becoming skilled enough to shape her own life, stroke by stroke.

Mariam asks Aminata to come along, saying it won't be late and she can still review her photos afterward. Aminata is standing at the gate, with her porridge money pouch heavy against her waist, and has to decide whether to accept.

Aminata is physically tired from waking at 4:30, stirring porridge, and plastering for two hours; her back and shoulder ache. She has not eaten since midday and hunger is beginning to pull at her. The cloth pouch of coins is heavy against her waist, reminding her of the day's sales.

Mariam's voice at the gate recalls an evening two weeks ago when Mariam coaxed her into sharing a bowl of fried plantains near the market, and she stayed later than planned, feeling drowsy the next morning during plaster practice. The sight of the metal gate also brings back the last tea-stall outing, when she paid for her own cup and then spent extra on a sweet she had not intended to buy.
